newsitem.title: INDIA: China says no nuclear arms sales to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: China says no nuclear arms sales to Pakistan.

text.p: China said on Friday it had sold no nuclear weapons-related technology or missiles to Pakistan and had no plans to do so.

"The Chinese government does not, did not, and will not sell or transfer any nuclear weapon or technology to any country," Shen Guofang, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, told a news briefing in New Delhi.
Shen, at a briefing on President Jiang Zemin's visit to India, was replying to a question on whether China had sold M-11 missiles to Pakistan, India's neighbour and traditional rival.
Earlier this month, the Washington Times reported that China recently sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tonnes of chemicals used to produce nerve agents.

Citing the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the paper said the reported transfer of missile-guidance components to Iran may violate Beijing's commitment to an international pact on curbing such sales.

In addition, some of the reported arms-technology transfers may violate a 1992 U.S. law that requires sanctions to be imposed on any nation exporting destabilising conventional weapons to Iran or Iraq, the newspaper said.
In October, the newspaper reported that China had sold nuclear weapons-related equipment to Pakistan, quoting a top-secret memorandum from the CIA.
Shen said: "We have some cooperation on peaceful utilisation of nuclear energy with Pakistan, but that is strictly supervised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)."
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda had expressed his concern during talks with Jiang over the number of sophisticated weapons flowing into the region, Shen added.
"He expressed the hope in a very broad sense that they do not hope such weapons flow in," Shen said.
"China does not own such advanced or sophisticated weapons and will not sell them to any country," he said.

India's concerns on Chinese supply of arms and nuclear collaboration had been raised in a "highly specific manner", Salman Haider, the highest ranking civil servant in India's Foreign Ministry, told reporters later.
"They are concerns of supply of sophisticated weapons to Pakistan and these were raised with Chinese ministers," he said.
"We also had concerns about the nature of nuclear cooperation between the two countries because we believe that Pakistan's nuclear programme is weapon-oriented," Haider added.

The United States and China negotiated for several months this year after revelations that China last year sold Pakistan ring magnets, which can be used in centrifuges that produce fuel for nuclear weapons.
Washington agreed in May not to impose sanctions, required by U.S. law, after accepting assurances by Chinese leaders that they were unaware of the sale carried out by a Chinese company.
President Bill Clinton's administration, eager to put ties with China on a more positive footing, has decided against imposing sanctions this year in several possible breaches of arms control pacts.
"I don't believe it is in the interests of China to sell advanced weapons to its neighbours," Shen said.
